title: Targeting Sodium Channel Subtypes to Treat Allergen-Induced Respiratory Symptoms
text:
Sensory nociceptive C-fiber nerves in the airways play a key role in mediating symptoms such as sneezing,
coughing, wheezing, and excessive secretions associated with allergic inflammation and respiratory viral
infections. This proposal aims to expand our knowledge of how these nerves are regulated, providing critical
insight for the development of novel C-fiber–targeted therapies aimed at quelling the symptoms of
inflammatory airway diseases.

title: Assessment of germline variants associated with immune-related adverse events following immune checkpoint inhibitors
text:
This research seeks to enhance public health by pinpointing genetic markers that can forecast who is at risk for
serious side effects from widely-used cancer immunotherapies, thereby enabling personalized treatment plans.
By investigating how these genetic factors interact with immunological and somatic variables, we aim to improve
the safety profile of these therapies, reducing healthcare burdens associated with treatment complications. The
project has the potential to minimize treatment-related complications on a broad scale, thereby enhancing the
overall quality of healthcare and contributing to a reduction in illness and disability across the population.

title: A Novel Multi-Lineage Human Intestinal Organoid Screening Platform for Drug Discovery and Preclinical Testing
text:
Over 90% of drug candidates fail in clinical trials due to the limitations of animal models and simple cell
cultures that fail to capture human intestinal complexity. Intero Biosystems has developed the first stem cell–
derived Human Intestinal Organoid (HIO) platform containing epithelium, fibroblasts, smooth muscle,
vasculature, and neurons, enabling scalable and reproducible assays for toxicity and fibrosis. This Phase II
project will optimize manufacturing and quality control, expand cytotoxicity and antifibrotic screening, and
position the HIO platform as a commercially viable tool to transform preclinical testing and accelerate drug
discovery.

title: Tau networks in AD psychosis
text:
This project aims to examine in vivo tau pathology in specific structural and functional
connectivity networks as mediator of psychotic symptoms in Alzheimer’s disease, which are
associated with a faster cognitive and functional decline and increased mortality.

title: A comprehensive approach to understanding the genetic causes of urinary stone disease: combining monogenic and polygenic analyses
text:
Urinary Stone Disease (USD) is a widespread ailment with significant health and economic impacts worldwide.
However, the mechanisms underlying the condition are still not fully understood, and effective prevention
strategies are lacking. This career development grant proposes to address these issues by employing
next-generation sequencing technology to systematically investigate both monogenic and polygenic genes
comprehensively and develop an integrated mono-polygenic risk model to facilitate precision medicine
interventions.

title: Expression of dystrophins with enhanced function
text:
This proposal addresses emerging limitations to approaches for gene therapy of DMD. Gene replacement
methods will be advanced by developing new methods to deliver larger dystrophins, while gene editing
approaches will be refined by applying multiple tools to advance editing into stem cells & the clinic.

title: Hybrid telehealth platform to facilitate dermatologist referrals through AI-assisted image screening and collaboration between hair professionals and dermatologists.
text: SOCAi Labs is developing a hybrid telehealth platform designed to facilitate collaboration between hair stylists and dermatologists for the early identification and referral of individuals with dermatologic concerns. Despite frequent interactions with clients, stylists remain an underutilized resource, with variable access to training and no established pathways for connecting clients to dermatologic care.  By equipping stylists with tools for early evaluation and streamlined referral, this platform aims to promote faster intervention and improved health outcomes for individuals who might otherwise be missed through traditional healthcare system.

title: Circuit control of motivation to take and seek alcohol
text:
Despite the prevalence and cost alcohol use disorder (AUD), treatment strategies are ineffective, especially in
preventing relapse. A key feature of AUD is that following long-term drinking, alcohol taking and seeking is
motivated by the drive to avoid alcohol’s withdrawal symptoms. This proposal focuses on understanding how
the brain controls the motivation to avoid the negative states induced by withdrawal and how we can use this
understanding to prevent relapse.

title: Multiplex Epitope Editing to Enable Novel Immunotherapies for Acute Myeloid Leukemia
text:
AML is the most common acute leukemia but, despite the diffuse use of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell
transplantation (HSCT), it still has the lowest survival rate of all leukemias. Adoptive immunotherapies are
currently hampered by the absence of specific targets, most of which are often shared with healthy tissues and
thus lead to immunosuppression/toxicity. Here, we will develop new gene editing strategies to generate a
“stealth” hematopoiesis that is resistant to immunoglobulin-based drugs/CAR-T cells. Our strategy allows
targeting multiple genes essential to leukemia survival, thus poorly amenable to escape mechanisms. It could
be rapidly implemented in allogeneic-HSCT protocols currently used as standard treatment for high-risk subtypes
of AML, like those with FLT3 mutation/ITD. Moreover, since our selected targets (FLT3, KIT and CD123) are
expressed at high levels in a spectrum of several hematologic malignancies, our strategy could provide more
efficacious yet less toxic therapeutic options for several blood cancers.

title: Mechanisms of adaptive immunity in RNA-targeting CRISPR-Cas13 systems
text:
RNA-guided RNA-targeting CRISPR-Cas13 systems provide antiphage defense through
collateral RNA damage by target-activated Cas13 effectors. We will investigate the specificity of
collateral RNA cleavage by various Cas13 homologs and how this cleavage mediates defense;
we will also explore how CRISPR-Cas13 systems acquire immunity. Our research will contribute
to a fundamental understanding of CRISPR-Cas13 functions and ultimately drive their use in
biomedical science and therapy.

title: Cell fusion and the role of syncytia in the response to epithelial damage
text:
In response to a wound, some cells fuse with several of their neighbors to become giant cells,
which move faster and close wounds faster than regular cells. Similar giant cells are observed
in many types of cancers, where they are malignant and resistant to therapy. We will
investigate how these giant cells form in response to wounds, how they function in wound
repair, and how they are eliminated after a wound is closed.

title: 9/10 Electrophysiology of Alcohol in Extended Amygdala
text:
INIA-N investigators have shown that brain immune-related pathways are involved in excessive
ethanol consumption and that pharmacological intervention with anti-inflammatory drugs reduces
drinking. This project will examine the cellular and synaptic mechanisms of alcohol-induced
immune responses in the brain that are hypothesized to contribute to excessive drinking.
Therefore, the present studies have the potential to identify new therapeutic targets to reduce
excessive drinking.

title: Examining the Role of Structural Factors in Cardiovascular Disease
text:
Evaluating causal mechanisms, temporality, and life-course exposures would advance current
understanding of CVD risk and support NIH’s commitment to addressing chronic health issues and
expanding the use of real-world data. The public health relevance is to inform future neighborhood-level
policies and practices for CVD prevention.

title: Development and validation of novel mouse models and expression vectors for characterizing severe alpha-thalassemia pathophysiology and evaluating gene therapy approaches.
text:
There are many patients of a-thalassemia, current therapies are insufficient for many of them and there are very
few studies on a-thalassemia; in addition, no severe mouse models are available to study this disease and to
test new therapies. Our goals are to generate new mouse models to investigate this understudied disease and
to test if a newly generated lentiviral vector that expresses the human a-globin gene can correct mice affected
by severe forms of a-thalassemia. Our proposed work will address these knowledge gaps by developing,
characterizing, and validating mouse models and gene therapy vectors for treating severe a-thalassemia.

title: Illuminating the chemical biology of stem cell decisions in plant roots
text:
Organ development relies on small signaling molecules, such as metabolites and lipids, that regulate cell behavior.
The primary goals of my research are to: 1) identify signaling molecules that regulate development, and 2)
investigate how cells sense and process these signals to make decisions.

title: Cancer Functional Imaging
text: The purpose of the Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center (SKCCC) Cancer Functional Imaging (CFI) Shared Resource (SR) is to provide comprehensive preclinical molecular and functional imaging infrastructure and expertise in multimodality imaging of cancer to support the preclinical imaging research needs of Center members. The original facility in the Miller Research Building houses a 9.4T MRI/S scanner for magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy, an intravital Olympus multiphoton microscope with in vivo imaging capability, a SuperArgus PET-CT scanner, a Vector SPECT scanner, and a Gamma Medica SPECT- CT scanner for nuclear imaging, optical imaging scanners (including an IVIS Spectrum and an LI COR near infrared scanner) and an ultrasound scanner. A state-of-the-art satellite facility in the SKCCC Cancer Research Building II (CRBII) in the lower basement opened in 2019 to house a simultaneous preclinical 7T PET-MR scanner. A photoacoustic imaging scanner, operational since November 2020, was also installed in CRBII- LB03 through an NIH High-End Instrument award. The CRBII-LB03 facility has allowed a much-needed expansion with new imaging equipment to maintain this SR as a state-of-the-art facility. It also is in close proximity to the newly installed mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) Rapiflex MALDI TOF/TOF scanner of the Mass Spectrometry Molecular Imaging and Multi-Omics SR, allowing investigation of the relationship between the in vivo imaging data and information provided by MSI. Because many of the imaging techniques are translatable to humans, imaging data generated through this SR can be used to develop translational applications in humans. Zaver Bhujwalla, Ph.D., is the Director of the CFI SR. She also is Program Co-Leader of the SKCCC Cancer Molecular and Functional Imaging (CMFI) Program and the Director of the Division of Cancer Imaging Research in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Science. Dr. Bhujwalla has an outstanding track record in molecular imaging applications in cancer. The two Associate Directors, Martin Pomper, M.D., Ph.D., and Dmitri Artemov, Ph.D., are well-known investigators who played a key role in the establishment of molecular imaging at The Johns Hopkins University. Dr. Pomper directs the Division of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging. He is also Co-Leader of the SKCCC CMFI Program. SKCCC Managed Shared Resource Reporting Period: January 1, 2020 to December 31, 2020

title: Addressing Shortcomings of AAV GeneTherapies for the Muscular Dystrophies
text:
This Wellstone Center will design and test improved AAV-mediated gene therapies for Duchenne and Limb
Girdle Muscular Dystrophy. The Center will also follow and evaluate muscular dystrophy patients who have
received an AAV gene therapy as well as patients prior to AAV treatment.

title: Ultrasensitive detection of circulating DNA methylation for head and neck cancer prognosis
text:
Despite improved treatment options, survival in patients with human papillomavirus-negative head and neck
cancer remains poor and there are critical barriers in the personalized management and therapy of this
challenging disease. Leveraging cutting-edge sequencing and novel analytical technologies developed by our
team, we propose the largest prospective cohort study investigating multimodal blood-based DNA methylation
makers for predicting individualized patient outcome. Findings will also lead to promising novel mechanisms
and signatures essential for the development of targeted therapies in the future.

title: Cell-specific role and therapeutic potential of KCa3.1 in atherosclerosis
text:
Heart attacks occur when either a coronary blockage grows to large or when a small blockage
“breaks” causing a blot clot to form, and since these potentially deadly plaques are small, often
the heart attack or stroke occurs without any warning or prior symptoms. Currently, we have very
few tools try to make a weak plaque stronger, so we want to identify the role of a particular set of
proteins that play a major role in determining both the size and strength of a coronary plaque. Our
evidence suggests that a currently available, FDA approved drug may meet this goal; therefore
the goal of this study will be to clearly identify how this target changes disease progression and
test the drug in a large animal model of coronary disease to pave the way for use in humans.

title: Deciphering the mechanisms underlying fibrotic remodeling of the bone marrow niche
text:
The focus of this proposal is to dissect “the seed and the soil” hypothesis explaining how mutated blood cells
communicate with their environment in the bone marrow during myelofibrosis. In myelofibrosis, blood cells
carrying mutations damage the bone marrow microenvironment that then produces excessive amount of scar
tissue (fibrous) in the bone marrow; fibrotic marrow is detrimental to normal blood cells and leads to anemia and
fatigue. We have identified the genes that regulate the fibrosis process and can serve as novel therapeutic
targets to ameliorate myelofibrosis.
